For comparable indices normalized to the same starting value, E = M − T is the level gap and s = E/M its share. The same annual premium is log((1 − s_start)/(1 − s_end)) / years. The rate, gap, and share describe related results on stated time bases. (§ The dynamics, stated explicitly)

Concentration under the stated model.

σ(t+1) = σ(t) + k·σ(t)·(1 − σ(t)),   0 < k < 1

With constant positive k and 0 &lt; σ(0) &lt; 1, the share rises toward one. Applying this model requires evidence for that persistent advantage; the equation itself does not establish an empirical law for all institutions. (§ The dynamics, stated explicitly)

The forward read — valuation to return.

CAPE ≈ 41  →  roughly −1 to −2.5%/yr real over the decade

The separate near-term readings of ≈3.8–3.9% nominal imply roughly 1% real after ≈2.5–3% inflation; the CAPE reading above is already real and spans a decade. (§4b)

Reproduce it

Run python -X utf8 reproduce_support.py for the supporting calculations named in the text, with network connections disabled. SUPPORTING_METHODS.md maps the results to their scripts and inputs; SUPPORTING_RESULTS.json records their output and hashes.

The analysis runs on public data (S&P 500 via public price feeds; economic series from FRED; inequality from the World Inequality Database and EPI; the labour share of GDP as the ILO's SDG 10.4.1 series fetched via Our World in Data (World: 53.9% in 2004 → 52.4% in 2024 — the series behind the ILO's $2.4-trillion counterfactual) with US labour share from FRED; historical lifespans from Wikidata; the long price record from Shiller's monthly S&P back to 1871; the deep-time seat migration from the Maddison Project's GDP-per-capita back to the 1300s), each fetched once and saved with a content hash so the exact inputs are pinned. Sources: Piketty–Saez (eml.berkeley.edu/~saez), EPI productivity–pay gap, ILO labour income share, FRED, US Census (migration, 2026), Brookings (immigration, Jan 2026), Robert Shiller (long S&P), the Maddison Project Database (long GDP/capita); historical pattern: Turchin and colleagues (cliodynamics / structural-demographic theory), the Seshat Global History Databank; pre-industrial inequality from Milanović–Lindert–Williamson ("Measuring Ancient Inequality," NBER w13550 / "Pre-Industrial Inequality," Economic Journal 2011) and pre-1913 US from Lindert–Williamson ("American Incomes 1774–1860," NBER w18396 / Unequal Gains, 2016), each cached with its source and read by inequality_maturity.py.

The figures reproduce from the pinned data, each printing its fitted numbers so they can be checked against the text: python draw_line.py → deliberate_line.png (the line + the flip); python draw_deep.py → migrating_seat.png (the migrating seat, 1300–2026); and python draw_all.py → deliberate_line_full.png (all three panels in one narrative image, with the within-society extraction wedge overlaid — the top-10% wealth share of Europe, 1300→2010: 64% (1300, pre-plague) → 47% (Black-Death trough) → 82% (1810) → 90% at its 1910 peak → 64% (2010). The points come from Alfani's own summary ("Europe's rich since 1300," VoxEU 2017, drawing on the EINITE project and Piketty 2014); since the page is now paywalled it was retrieved from a public web-archive snapshot and cached with its source, so every point is traceable to Alfani's stated figures rather than invented. The series itself is the one Alfani still publishes — "Inequality in History: A Long-Run View," Stone Center Working Paper 74 (2023), Fig. 2.1(a), where pre-unification "Italy" is the average of four states (the Sabaudian and Florentine States, the Republic of Venice, and the Kingdom of Naples/Apulia), built from Alfani 2021 (JEL) for 1300–1810 and Alfani & Schifano 2021 for 1820–2010; its stylized fact is the one this figure draws: inequality grew for most of seven centuries, with two reversals — the century after the Black Death and 1914 to the mid-1970s. The 2023 paper is the source reference; the exact tabulated values behind its chart are in the closed 2021 article, so the numbers here remain the summary's until that table is read.)

Finally, python draw_forward.py → forward_line.png carries the post-1971 line forward to 2030: the record stretch, the weak window and how it closes (the grind-or-release fork), and the deliberate flip — every fitted number printed on the figure, from forward_derivation.py and forward_sim.py.

The central connection is the premium and its continued collection. Ownership rules specify the claims, people and public offices maintain and enforce them, and holders receive the resulting premium. That is the operation this paper asks the reader to inspect. Changing who occupies an office can leave collection unchanged; changing the rules can change who receives the result. The proposed alternative is therefore stated in terms of contribution, allocation, and publicly checkable accounting.

The findings, the math, and the model are written in ordinary terms, computed from public data, and free to check, use, and interpret. That was the point of writing it plainly. The line was never anyone's to own. It was always everyone's.
